items.diagram_kind: Cartesian square for Poincare-bundle base change along the Mumford isogeny
items.reason: Proof step 2.1 explicitly invokes a Cartesian square, and its geometric base change isomorphism is central to identifying the direct image as O_{K(L)}[-g]. A displayed square would make the two projections and the pullback unambiguous. The current render contains no such square.

claim_lines.text: 2.1 Consider the Cartesian square with $\varphi=\varphi_{\mathcal L}$, the morphism $(\operatorname{id}\times\varphi):A\times_kA\to A\times_kA^\vee$, and projections $p_2:A\times_kA\to A$ and $p_2:A\times_kA^\vee\to A^\vee$. By flat base change [F4] applied to [F1] we have $Rp_{2,*}((\operatorname{id}\times\varphi)^*\mathcal P)\cong\varphi^*(Rp_{2,*}\mathcal P)\cong\varphi^*(k(0)[-g])\cong\mathcal O_{K(\mathcal L)}[-g]$, where $\varphi^{-1}(0)=K(\mathcal L)$ is finite of length $\deg\varphi$ by [F2]. Since $(\operatorname{id}\times\varphi)^*\mathcal P\cong\Lambda(\mathcal L)$ by [F2], the direct images of $\Lambda(\mathcal L)$ under $p_2$ vanish except in degree $g$, where they equal $\mathcal O_{K(\mathcal L)}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct]

arrows: top horizontal id_A × φ_L: A ×_k A → A ×_k A^∨
left vertical p_2: A ×_k A → A
right vertical p_2: A ×_k A^∨ → A^∨
labels: on the upper-right product use the Poincare bundle P; its pullback to the upper-left product is Λ(L)
the fibre over 0 ∈ A^∨ is K(L)=φ_L^{-1}(0) ⊂ A, so base change identifies the derived direct image with O_{K(L)}[-g]
checks: The top-left object is the fibre product A ×_{A^∨} (A × A^∨), using φ_L on the lower-left factor and p_2 on the upper-right factor; the canonical isomorphism sends (x,y) to ((x,y),(x,φ_L(y))) in the fibre product, with product coordinates ordered as in id × φ_L.
Both paths from A × A to A^∨ equal φ_L ∘ p_2 = p_2 ∘ (id × φ_L); the square commutes.
The base-change input is the finite-flat morphism φ_L established in proof step 1.1, not merely finiteness of its kernel as a set.
Use scheme-theoretic K(L), retaining nonreduced structure and length; do not depict it as only the set of geometric kernel points.
The degree shift is [-g], so the only nonzero direct image sheaf occurs in degree g.

items.diagram_kind: Complete flag incidence locus in a product of Grassmannians
items.reason: The statement and step 1.1 identify the flag variety with a closed incidence locus in a product, while the current display only writes the nested subspaces. A compact incidence diagram could show how a point of the flag variety projects to its Grassmannian factors and how adjacent inclusions cut out the closed locus. This is an editorial aid; the existing formula and proof already state the construction accurately.

claim_lines.text: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space of dimension $n\ge1$. The set $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$ of complete flags

carries the structure of a smooth projective classical $k$-variety: it is the closed subvariety of the product of Grassmannians $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbf{Gr}_i(V)$ cut out by the incidence conditions $V_i\subseteq V_{i+1}$, embedded in a product of projective spaces by Pl\u00fccker coordinates. The group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ acts transitively on $\mathrm{Fl}(V)$, the stabilizer of a flag is a closed subgroup scheme of $\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and the stabilizer of a complete flag is solvable.

[F3] Incidence is closed: for $1\le i\le n-1$ the set $\{(W,W')\in\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)\times\operatorname{Gr}(i+1,V):W\subseteq W'\}$ is a closed subvariety of the product. In a standard affine chart of $\operatorname{Gr}(i+1,V)$ in which $W'$ is spanned by the rows of a matrix whose first $i+1$ columns form the identity, a complement of the chart locus is given by the vanishing of the Pl\u00fccker coordinate, and $W\subseteq W'$ is expressed by the linear equations saying that a spanning matrix of $W$ has zero entries in the coordinates complementary to $W'$; these equations are polynomial in the chart coordinates of $W$ and glue over the charts of $\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)$. (Milne, Proposition 7.30, printed p. 146. No local item isolates this incidence statement.)

1.1 For $n=1$, the empty product is the one-point variety, there is a unique flag, and all incidence conditions are vacuous. For $n>1$, by [F1] each $\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)$ is a projective variety, and by [F2] the product $P=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{Gr}(i,V)$ is a projective variety. By [F3] each incidence condition $V_i\subseteq V_{i+1}$ defines a closed subvariety, so their intersection $\mathrm{Fl}(V)\subseteq P$ is a closed subvariety; by [F4] it is projective, hence complete, and its Pl\u00fccker embedding in the product of projective spaces is the restriction of the Pl\u00fccker embeddings of the factors. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

nodes: for each 1 ≤ i < n−1, the pair product Gr_i(V) × Gr_{i+1}(V)
the adjacent incidence subvariety Inc_i = {(W_i,W_{i+1}) : W_i ⊆ W_{i+1}}
arrows_and_relations: coordinate projections π_i: Fl(V) → Gr_i(V), sending a flag to V_i
for each adjacent pair i,i+1, (π_i,π_{i+1}) factors through Inc_i ↪ Gr_i(V) × Gr_{i+1}(V)
the defining locus is the intersection of the inverse images of Inc_i over all adjacent i
checks: Factors are exactly Gr_i(V) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n−1; V_0=0 and V_n=V are fixed endpoints, not extra Grassmannian factors.

Adjacent incidence conditions are V_i ⊆ V_{i+1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ n−2 in the product; the endpoints are automatic. For n=1 the product is a point and there are no incidence conditions; for n=2 there is one factor and no adjacent pair condition.
Each Inc_i is a closed subvariety, so their common locus is closed in P. Do not suggest arbitrary independent Grassmannian points form a flag.
Projection arrows have codomain Gr_i(V); if included in a pair-product panel, the paired projection lands in Inc_i only on Fl(V).
